newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parties edge closer to EMU budget accord.
newsitem.headline: German parties edge closer to EMU budget accord.

text.p: Germany's squabbling coalition partners appeared close to agreement on Tuesday over the burning question of how to reduce the country's budget deficit.
The issue -- revolving around whether to raise taxes -- has driven a wedge between government allies and is widely seen as having weakened the standing of Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) have been holding a series of meetings with its pro-business Free Democrat (FDP) partners over the issue.
"We are not at the end of the talks, but we moving in the right direction and it could happen fast," said Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of the FDP.
"The budget consolidation will succeed without tax increases," he added.
The FDP and the CDU will meet again in Bonn on Wednesday.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, the CDU's parliamentary group leader, said the coalition had agreed on the goal of cutting tax rates, but said there was also a broad consensus that the government could not afford to ignore the possibility of lower tax revenues.

Failure to cut the deficit has reduced the chances that Germany will meet fiscal requirements for European economic and monetary union. The Maastricht Treaty permits budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
Some newspapers on Tuesday still portrayed the government partners as no nearer to solving an issue which has strained the coalition for months.
"It is still far from clear how they will get out of this big mess," Handelsblatt daily wrote in an editorial.

"Running about like a bunch of chickens with their heads cut off, coalition leaders are cackling over high debts, fast privatisations, cutbacks and higher taxes. The government is grabbing at straws."

The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) said there was a growing number of government party members opposed to Kohl and his uncompromising determination to bring Germany into a single currency in 1999.
Anti-euro hardliners believe that forcing the government to keep its word on cutting the deficit to 3.0 percent of GDP will topple Kohl should Germany fail to make the grade.
"They are forming in Bavaria and their weapon could be called 3.0," the influential daily said.

The FAZ added that those conservative party members promoting such a shakeup were well aware of the fact that it could mean the CDU would no longer have Kohl to carry its banner into the next election due in 1998.
"Kohl can only run again as chancellor of the euro," the FAZ said, suggesting if EMU collapses then Kohl's declaration to run for an unprecedented fifth term in 1998 would be scrapped.
But the opposition Social Democrats, gaining in popularity and reluctant to assist Kohl's 14-year-old government out of the jam, turned up the volume on its calls for early elections.
Gerhard Schroeder, the premier of Lower Saxony who may be the SPD's challenger to Kohl, said the CDU/FDP government had clearly run out of ideas and should resign.

"The coalition has reached its end," Schroeder told NDR radio. "They have run out of ideas and people. It is thus time for the chancellor to clear the way for new elections. That would be the responsible thing to do."

Schroeder, who opinion polls say would handily beat Kohl, said the SPD would have no trouble picking a candidate to challenge Kohl. He said the SPD, which has lost four straight polls to Kohl, would have a candidate within hours.

"If Helmut Kohl acts responsibly and calls early elections, we would settle the question of who would run for chancellor within a few hours," said Schroeder, who along with SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine are the party's two leading candidates.
